paragraphs.heading: When oxygen first built up
paragraphs.text: The Great Oxidation Event, or GOE, was a stretch of the Paleoproterozoic era when free oxygen first started to rise in Earth's air and shallow seas. It goes by several other names, including the Oxygen Catastrophe and the Oxygen Revolution. It began around 2.46 to 2.426 billion years ago, in the Siderian period, and wound down near 2.06 billion years ago, in the Rhyacian. By its end, oxygen may have reached as much as 10% of the level in today's air.

paragraphs.heading: Reducing and oxidizing air
paragraphs.text: Before the event, the atmosphere was weakly reducing. That means it was mostly N₂ and CO₂, plus traces of water vapor, methane, hydrogen and carbon monoxide, and almost no oxygen at all. Today's air is about 21% oxygen, which makes it an oxidizing atmosphere. The GOE was the switch from the first kind to the second.

paragraphs.heading: Tiny makers of oxygen
paragraphs.text: The likely cause was cyanobacteria. These microbes evolved photosynthesis based on chlorophyll, which splits water and gives off dioxygen, O₂, as a byproduct. They may have appeared as early as 3.5 billion years ago. Geological, isotopic and chemical evidence suggests their oxygen began to collect in the Archean atmosphere. For close to a billion years the steady supply was soaked up by ferrous iron, sulfur, hydrogen sulfide and methane at the surface, until that capacity to absorb it was used up.

paragraphs.heading: A poison for early life
paragraphs.text: Free oxygen is highly reactive and can damage organic compounds, especially genetic material, so it was toxic to a living world that was then mostly anaerobic. It may have wiped out many early organisms, mainly archaea living in colonies. Together with a global glaciation, the change wrecked microbial mats across the planet. Isotope data from sulfate minerals have been read as showing that the biosphere shrank by more than 80% at the close of the GOE. Even so, the event is usually left off the standard lists of great extinctions, which in practice only cover the Phanerozoic eon.

paragraphs.heading: A new path for life
paragraphs.text: Some archaea survived by teaming up with aerobic proteobacteria through symbiogenesis. Those bacteria moved inside their hosts and became mitochondria. That partnership may explain how eukaryotic organisms arose, and later how many-celled life evolved.

paragraphs.heading: Reading oxygen in the rocks
paragraphs.text: Much of what we know started with the American geologist Preston Cloud in the 1970s. He noticed that sediments older than about 2 billion years held grains of pyrite, uraninite and siderite, minerals that oxygen quickly destroys and that younger sediments lack. Around the same time, red beds, colored by the iron mineral hematite, start to show up in the record. Banded iron formation peaked about 2.5 billion years ago and had mostly vanished by 1.85 billion years ago. Because these rocks need dissolved iron carried into basins, and oxygen-rich water stops that, their end is taken to mark when the deep ocean gained oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: An open question of timing
paragraphs.text: Most researchers agree that the air first gained oxygen sometime in the first half of the Paleoproterozoic, but the exact date is disputed. Papers published between 2016 and 2022 placed the start anywhere from 2.7 to 2.3 billion years ago, a spread of about 500 million years. Part of the problem is that the sedimentary record from this era is incomplete. The ages of many ancient rock layers are also uncertain, and different chemical clues can be read in different ways.
